title: Apple Crumble
subtitle: Baked apples under a crisp oat and butter topping
excerpt: Sharp cooking apples softened in brown sugar and cinnamon, topped with a buttery oat crumble and baked until golden and bubbling. The quintessential British autumn pudding.

recipe.sourceNotes: Apple crumble was invented in Britain during the Second World War as a practical alternative to apple pie, at a time when the pastry ingredients were rationed. The crumble topping uses less fat and flour than pastry and was therefore a more economical use of limited ingredients. It quickly became more popular than pie among home bakers and has remained so. The addition of oats to the topping is a post-war development that gives extra crunch. Bramley apples are the traditional choice: they are specifically bred for cooking and break down to a fluffy purée under the crumble, contrasting with the crunchy top. Served with custard, cream, or ice cream.

recipeTools.notes: A 25 cm oven-proof ceramic baking dish.

content.text: The crumble topping should be rubbed together with cold butter and handled minimally: the goal is a mixture of fine crumbs and larger, irregular clumps, which gives the topping texture when baked. Do not over-rub or it will become too fine and smooth. Press the topping gently onto the fruit without compacting it. The crumble is done when the edges are visibly bubbling and the top is well coloured.

items.preparation: Bramley or Granny Smith, peeled, cored, and sliced

content.text: Heat the oven to 190 C / fan 170 C / gas 5. Toss the sliced apples with 80 g brown sugar, cinnamon, and lemon juice. Spread in a baking dish.
Rub together the flour, oats, cold butter, 100 g brown sugar, and salt with your fingertips until the mixture forms large, uneven clumps. Do not overwork.

Scatter the crumble topping evenly over the apple. Press very lightly. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the topping is golden and the apple juices are bubbling around the edges. Rest for 5 minutes. Serve warm with custard, cream, or vanilla ice cream.
